parts.f-P17j: Create a no-secrets rule. No grownup has a right to ask a kid to keep a secret from their mom or another trusted adult, whether it's about a gift, a game, a touch, a conversation or a relationship. A surprise isn't a secret, because at the end of a certain date it has to be told. But secrets meant to isolate a kid aren't allowed.
parts.f-P17k: Create a no-secrets rule. No grownup has a right to ask a kid to keep a secret from their mom or another trusted adult, whether it's about a gift, a game, a touch, a conversation or a relationship. A surprise has an end date. But isolating a kid with secrets isn't allowed.
parts.f-P18j: Teach truthfulness before there's a crisis. Talk with the kids about the importance of telling the truth, the power of their words, and how what they say will be taken seriously. Don't let the teaching turn into interrogation, punishment when they're not sure, or a reason to brush off what they report. A scared or confused kid may tell it badly and still need protection.
parts.f-P25b5: Kids also need a good set of transferable skills and education, good relationships with people outside the community, access to their own records and documents, and at least one plausible next step outside the community (school, an apprenticeship, work, family, another community). It would be great if the community could also provide resources to smooth the transition, like temporary housing, travel expenses, tools or a little money, but even if it can't, it can at least not make things worse by punishing people for leaving, or by holding back knowledge or records a young adult would need to function outside the community. No upbringing can provide perfect freedom, and the point isn't to erase path dependence. It's to not turn belonging into a trap.

parts.f-P3i: All of this will ultimately be reviewed by the kids, once they're grown, and their review weighs more heavily than founders usually want it to. Adults can go on about their intentions forever, but the kids who lived it might have something else to say.
parts.f-P3k: All of this will ultimately be reviewed by the kids who grew up with it, and their review weighs more heavily than founders usually want it to. Adults can go on about their intentions forever, but the kids might have something else to say.
parts.f-P2b: I mention vaccination specifically because it's one of the values I would absolutely need to share with people in a community, if I was going to raise children there. I'm not trying to design a village for everyone, only saying that communities need some common ground among the parents on children's health, enough that they can actually trust one another.
parts.f-P16b: Give children real agency. When kids say no, it counts, and no grownup has a right to their affection, physical contact, obedience outside of legitimate safety needs, or private access to them.
parts.f-P26: It's possible that some of them will leave permanently, and others will start their own communities with different values rather than wait decades to inherit the original one. And parents may experience that as a loss, even when it's the movement evolving.
